name: Agreement with the Jicarilla Apache of December 10, 1873 (San Juan reservation)
promises: A reservation on the San Juan River, bounded by the southern line of Colorado and the eastern line of the Navajo reservation, closed to unauthorised persons (Article 1).
The Jicarilla were to give up claims outside it and move there once Congress ratified the agreement (Article 2).
The United States was to appropriate $10,000 a year for five years, then $3,000 a year for ten years for education (Article 3).
The agreement was expressly subject to ratification or rejection by Congress.
today: The President set the tract apart on March 25, 1874 "subject to action of Congress" and cancelled that order on July 18, 1876. The Indian Claims Commission found in Docket 22-A (1963) that the Jicarilla were deprived of their aboriginal title gradually, with no single date of taking, and without payment; the land claim was settled for $9,150,000 in 1971.

openQuestions: No source opened states in so many words that Congress never ratified this agreement; Royce and the March 25, 1874 order call it subject to Congress, and the reserve was cancelled in 1876. If a source confirms non-ratification, the status should be "unratified".

The Docket 22-A finding of a gradual taking of Jicarilla aboriginal land (1963) is not tied to this agreement; which Jicarilla record should carry it (for example the 1887 reservation order) is unsettled. It is not counted here.
The Jicarilla Apache Nation's own account was not searched in this pass.
